short_description: Dried pigeon droppings, common on balconies, window ledges and air-conditioner units in cities. This test looks for IgE, the allergy antibody, against it. It shows whether your immune system recognises it, not whether you are allergic.
exposure_context: Waste from pigeons, which can dry and mix into dust around balconies, roofs and bird cages.
what_happens_inside_my_body: Your immune system protects you by making antibodies, proteins that recognise things it sees as a threat.
In allergies, it makes an antibody called IgE against something that is usually harmless.
When IgE meets that substance again, it can trigger symptoms such as sneezing, itching, rashes, swelling or wheezing.
why_this_test_matters: This test can help a doctor decide whether Pigeon Droppings might be linked to symptoms such as sneezing, itchy eyes, wheezing or skin rashes around animals or birds.

assay_unconfirmed: The lab has not confirmed the test method or how this result is reported, so CURA does not label it positive or negative. A positive allergy antibody result means your immune system recognises Pigeon Droppings. It does not prove you will react to it.

positive_or_elevated: Antibodies to Pigeon Droppings were found. This is called sensitisation. Many sensitised people have no symptoms, so it matters only if you react when exposed.
negative_or_low: Little or no antibody to Pigeon Droppings was found. This makes an IgE allergy less likely, but does not rule out every kind of reaction.

possible_influencing_factors: Exact test method and material used
Timing and type of symptoms after contact

clinical_limitations: An allergy antibody test cannot confirm an allergy on its own or predict how severe a reaction might be. A doctor reads it alongside what happens when you are exposed.

When IgE meets that substance again, it can trigger symptoms such as sneezing, itching, rashes, swelling or wheezing.
why_this_test_matters: This test can help a doctor decide whether Cabbage might be linked to symptoms such as hives, itching, swelling, tummy upset or wheezing after eating.

assay_unconfirmed: The lab has not confirmed the test method or how this result is reported, so CURA does not label it positive or negative. A positive allergy antibody result means your immune system recognises Cabbage. It does not prove you will react to it.

positive_or_elevated: Antibodies to Cabbage were found. This is called sensitisation. Many sensitised people have no symptoms, so it matters only if you react when exposed.
negative_or_low: Little or no antibody to Cabbage was found. This makes an IgE allergy less likely, but does not rule out every kind of reaction.

possible_influencing_factors: Exact test method and material used
Timing and type of symptoms after contact
Antibodies to similar substances
clinical_limitations: An allergy antibody test cannot confirm an allergy on its own or predict how severe a reaction might be. A doctor reads it alongside what happens when you are exposed.

assay_unconfirmed: Where might I come across Cabbage?
Does a positive Cabbage test mean I am allergic to it?
Do I need to stop eating Cabbage?
What symptoms would an allergy to Cabbage cause?

diet_and_lifestyle: Avoiding a food matters only if it causes symptoms. Many people with antibodies to a food eat it without any problem.
everyday_support: Do not cut Cabbage or other foods from your diet based on this result alone. Unnecessary avoidance can limit nutrition, especially for children.
If you notice symptoms after eating Cabbage, note what you ate, how much and how soon symptoms began. This helps a doctor judge whether the result matters.
when_to_seek_medical_advice: Talk to a doctor or allergy specialist if you get symptoms after eating Cabbage.
Seek emergency care straight away for swelling of the face, eyes or tongue, a hoarse or whispered voice, trouble breathing or wheezing, dizziness or collapse after contact with any trigger.

When IgE meets that substance again, it can trigger symptoms such as sneezing, itching, rashes, swelling or wheezing.
why_this_test_matters: This test can help a doctor decide whether Yeast might be linked to symptoms such as hives, itching, swelling, tummy upset or wheezing after eating.

assay_unconfirmed: The lab has not confirmed the test method or how this result is reported, so CURA does not label it positive or negative. A positive allergy antibody result means your immune system recognises Yeast. It does not prove you will react to it.

positive_or_elevated: Antibodies to Yeast were found. This is called sensitisation. Many sensitised people have no symptoms, so it matters only if you react when exposed.
negative_or_low: Little or no antibody to Yeast was found. This makes an IgE allergy less likely, but does not rule out every kind of reaction.

possible_influencing_factors: Exact test method and material used
Timing and type of symptoms after contact
Antibodies to similar substances
clinical_limitations: An allergy antibody test cannot confirm an allergy on its own or predict how severe a reaction might be. A doctor reads it alongside what happens when you are exposed.

Do I need to stop eating Yeast?

when_to_seek_medical_advice: Talk to a doctor or allergy specialist if you get symptoms after eating Yeast.
